# Witness Camera: full text of key pages

Witness Camera (App Store name: Witness: Camera Beyond Reach) is a free iPhone and Android app for documenting police encounters. It records with the screen black and uploads every 15 seconds to storage the user owns. Index of all pages: https://witnesscamera.com/llms.txt

# Filming the police at student protests across Europe
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/filming-police-student-protests-europe

Filming the police at student protests across Europe

What is happening, what stays the same everywhere, and where to find the guide for your country.

Since mid-September 2026, school pupils and university students have been protesting across Europe over teacher shortages, school buildings, housing and fees. In some places there have been clashes with police, tear gas and arrests, many of them of minors. Plenty of people are filming a police intervention in a crowd for the first time. This page collects the verified facts and points to a country guide in each language. It takes no side on the demands or on the violence reported on either side. Its purpose is documenting what happens, whoever is in the wrong.

 Short answer. Filming police on duty in a public place is generally protected in the countries we cover (France, Italy, Germany, Greece, Spain). The real risk is physically obstructing an intervention, not the camera. Germany is the exception to watch: sound is the legal risk there (section 201 StGB), and Witness always records sound. As of 21 October 2026, school and student protests with police involvement are reported in France, Italy, Greece and, announced for 31 October, Germany; Spain has a teachers' strike and Portugal a tuition protest. Witness Camera is a free iPhone and Android app that uploads every 15 seconds to storage you own. This is not legal advice.

## What is happening, country by country

As of 21 October 2026, from press reports, with figures attributed to whoever gave them. They change quickly and often disagree.

 - France. A pupil and student movement that began at a school in Créteil in September has spread nationwide. On 13 October the Interior Ministry counted 161,500 demonstrators and the youth unions 480,000, and police used tear gas (Radio-Canada). Time reports over 6,000 arrests, 87% of those detained being minors, citing the Justice Ministry. Guide in French.

 - Italy. On 16 October, the "No Meloni Day", students marched in at least twelve cities. In Turin, stones and torches were thrown at police, who responded with water cannon and some tear gas, and the Turin police headquarters reported three minors arrested for aggravated resistance (ANSA). A general strike is called for 30 October and a European student strike for 20 November. Guide in Italian.

 - Germany. Nationwide school protests are announced for 31 October. The organisers, "GenZ regelt", say they reject violence and claim more than 10,000 registrations in 21 cities. A Federal Interior Ministry spokesperson said security agencies are monitoring the calls (News4teachers). Guide in German.

 - Greece. Students have camped in Athens' Syntagma Square since 13 October over housing and study costs, with a rally at the Propylaia on 21 October (Greek press). In the coverage we found there were no clashes with police. Guide in Greek.

 - Spain. This is mainly a teachers' strike, not a student protest: an indefinite strike in Madrid's public schools since 14 October, with a march from Atocha on 22 October (El Diario de Madrid). Student and family organisations are reported to be joining (El Economista). Guide in Spanish.

 - Portugal. Student associations in Lisbon called a protest on 21 October against the Government's proposal to unfreeze tuition fees from 2027/28 (Observador). We found no reports of police incidents. We do not yet have a Portugal-specific legal guide.

We found no comparable student street protests in the Netherlands, Poland, Romania or Sweden, so there are no guides for them in this series. The general guides for those countries are linked from Filming the police in Europe.

## What stays the same everywhere

 - The law protects filming, not obstructing. Across the countries above, standing at a reasonable distance with the phone visible is generally protected. Physically getting in the way of an intervention is the real risk, camera or not. The country pages have the details, with sources. None of this is legal advice.

 - A crowd is a different job. Stay at the edge, know two exits, film the calm first, say the time aloud every few minutes. See How to film at a protest.

 - Expect the network to fail. Mobile networks saturate in a crowd. Anything that depends on a live connection should queue on the phone and send when it can.

 - Many protesters are minors. Documenting is one thing, publishing is another. Keep the original untouched, and blur the faces of minors and bystanders before posting anything.

 - Prepare beforehand. Passcode instead of biometrics, a full battery, a lawyer's number written on your arm, and a test recording before the day.

## Coming up

As of 26 October 2026, from press reports. Dates, places and times move, and calls circulating on social media are often unreliable. Confirm with the organisers and the authorities.

 - Italy, 30 October. A 24-hour general strike called by USB, registered with the transport ministry on 6 October. Marches in cities are expected, but we found no confirmed city list. New in Italy: decree-law 190/2026, in force from 23 October, creates an offence of organised violence in demonstrations and allows arrests within 48 hours on the basis of video, including of minors; it must be converted into law within 60 days. That makes handling of raw footage more sensitive. On 20 November, CGIL has called its own general strike and the Collettivo Osa has announced a European student strike. Guide in Italian.

 - Germany, Saturday 31 October. School protests announced under the names "Gen Z steht auf" and "Gen Z regelt", in cities including Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich. The Berlin police are preparing a large operation, and according to the Tagesspiegel many cities had no registered assembly yet, with conflicting times and meeting points online. Guide in German.

 - France, Thursday 5 November. A national strike and demonstrations called by UNSA, CFDT, CGT, FO and FSU over wages and public services, backing the pupil and student movement. Pupils are on the Toussaint holiday until 2 November. We found no officially declared gathering in Paris for 31 October. Guide in French.

 - Greece, 17 November. The annual march for the Athens Polytechnic anniversary. Last year's march was estimated by the police at more than 15,000 people, with a large police presence and, according to several outlets, preventive detentions. The 2026 arrangements had not been announced. Guide in Greek.

 - Spain, 20 and 21 November. An international student and youth strike on 20 November promoted by the Sindicato de Estudiantes, a demonstration in Catalonia on 21 November and strikes there from 26 November, while Madrid's indefinite education strike continues. Guide in Spanish.

## Where guides differ

The French digital-investigation NGO Index publishes Filmer la police : avant, pendant, après (updated 15 October 2026, in French). Some of its advice differs from ours.

 - Speaking aloud. Index advises against commenting, so the soundtrack keeps what officers say and does not identify you. Other guides advise saying the time and place at key moments. Our view: if you worry your voice would identify you, stay silent. If you speak, stick to the time and what you see. Witness records sound either way.

 - Location. Index advises against switching GPS on. Witness writes location into each recording's chain-of-custody record if you allow it, which ties footage to a place. You can decline location and everything else still works. Decide before the day.

 - Live broadcasting. Index advises against filming live. Witness does not broadcast: it sends private pieces to storage you own. That is not the same as a public live stream.

 - Where all the guides agree: stay several metres back, film wide with a visible landmark, avoid digital zoom, hold the phone horizontally, never edit the original, film with others from different angles, and do not publish at once.

## Where Witness fits

Witness records with the screen black and uploads every 15 seconds to a storage account you own, so what was already sent survives a seized or smashed phone. Each piece is hashed and the session is time-stamped, and anyone can verify the footage without the app. It does not replace a lawyer, does not make anything lawful that is not, and does not protect you physically.

 One caution for Germany. Witness always records sound, and the app has no setting to turn the microphone off. German law treats recording the non-publicly spoken word as an offence (section 201 of the Strafgesetzbuch), and whether an officer's announcement at a public operation counts is disputed. The German guide explains this. If you want to work without sound, Witness is currently the wrong tool for that.

## Questions

### Can you film the police at a student protest in Europe?

 In France, Italy, Germany, Greece and Spain, filming police on duty in a public place is generally protected, and the real limit is physically obstructing an intervention. Germany treats recording the non-publicly spoken word as an offence (section 201 StGB), so sound is the risk there. This is not legal advice, and the country guides give the sources.

### Which European countries have student or school protests right now?

 As of 21 October 2026: France (a nationwide pupil and student movement since September), Italy (the 16 October “No Meloni Day”), Germany (school protests announced for 31 October), Greece (students camping in Syntagma Square over housing), Spain (a teachers' strike in Madrid) and Portugal (a tuition protest in Lisbon). We found no comparable student street protests in the Netherlands, Poland, Romania or Sweden.

### How can I keep my footage if police take my phone?

 Use an app that uploads while you record. Witness Camera records with the screen black and uploads a piece every 15 seconds to a cloud account you own, so footage already sent is safe. The piece being recorded and any queued pieces are on the phone.

### Does Witness record sound?

 Yes, always. Witness has no setting to turn the microphone off. In Germany, where recording the non-publicly spoken word is an offence, that matters, and if you want to work without sound Witness is currently the wrong tool.

### Is Witness free?

 Yes. Witness Camera (App Store name: Witness: Camera Beyond Reach) is free on iPhone (iOS 17 and later) and Android (11 and later). An optional paid Pro tier adds capture quality, nothing that protects footage.

# Protest phone checklist: 10 steps before you film the police
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/protest-phone-checklist

Protest phone checklist: 10 steps before you film the police

What to do in the hour before you leave, in the order that matters.

Most footage of protests is lost for boring reasons: a dead battery, a locked-out phone, uploads that never started, a phone taken before anything was saved. This checklist is the preparation that prevents those. It applies to school and university protests across Europe and to any other demonstration.

 Short answer. Before a protest: set a six-digit passcode instead of Face ID, charge to 100% and carry a power bank, connect cloud storage and test-record for 30 seconds, name an emergency contact, write a lawyer's number on your arm, and know two exits. Witness Camera is a free iPhone and Android app that records with the screen black and uploads every 15 seconds, so footage already sent survives a seized phone.

## The ten steps

 - Use a passcode, not biometrics. Set a passcode of at least six digits instead of Face ID or a fingerprint. On iPhone, holding the side button and a volume button together forces the passcode screen.

 - Charge to 100% and bring a power bank. Filming on a congested network with continuous upload is the worst case for a battery, and demonstrations run long.

 - Connect your own storage. In Witness, connect Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud or WebDAV. Footage uploads to an account you own. There is no Witness server and no account with the developer.

 - Test it for 30 seconds. Record half a minute, stop, and check that the file appears in your storage. Do this the day before, not at the protest.

 - Name an emergency contact. Each recording is shared with the contact you name as it is made, so someone else has your material if you are detained.

 - Set up instant start. iPhone: Action Button (iPhone 15 Pro and newer), Lock Screen widget or a Siri phrase. Android: Quick Settings tile, home-screen widget or an assistant shortcut.

 - Write a lawyer's number on your arm. In marker, on skin. A number stored in the phone is unreachable if the phone is taken. Use a lawyer or legal-support group you trust.

 - Tell the people you go with. If you are there to film, say so, so nobody expects you to be somewhere else when it matters.

 - Plan two exits and stay at the edge. The edge of a crowd shows the line, the crowd and the space between them. The middle gives you no exit and no context.

 - Decide now what you will publish. Keep the original untouched. Before posting anything online, blur the faces of minors and bystanders. Many protesters are under 18.

## If you are in Germany, decide about sound first

Witness always records sound and has no setting to turn the microphone off. German law treats recording the non-publicly spoken word as an offence (section 201 of the Strafgesetzbuch), and whether an officer's announcement at a public operation counts is disputed. Our German legal page explains it. If you want to work without sound, Witness is currently the wrong tool.

## What the checklist cannot do

It will not make recording lawful where it is not, protect you physically, or guarantee that a court or newsroom accepts your footage. The law differs by country: see Filming the police at student protests across Europe. This is not legal advice.

## Questions

### What should I do with my phone before a protest?

 Set a six-digit passcode instead of biometrics, charge it fully and carry a power bank, connect cloud storage and test-record for 30 seconds, name an emergency contact, and write a lawyer's number on your arm.

### Will uploads work in a crowd?

 Mobile networks often saturate at large demonstrations. Witness keeps each piece on the phone until your storage confirms it, and uploads when a connection is available, rather than failing.

### What if my phone is taken?

 Pieces that had already uploaded are safe in your own cloud storage. The piece being recorded and any pieces still queued are on the phone, so the practical loss is whatever had not finished sending.

### Do I need a special app to film at a protest?

 No. Any camera app works for filming. Witness adds black-screen recording, uploads every 15 seconds to storage you own, SHA-256 hashing and an independent time-stamp. It is free on iPhone and Android.

# Police ask you to delete your protest video or take your phone: Europe
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/police-ask-you-to-delete-video-protest-europe

Police told you to delete your video or hand over your phone at a protest

A calm sequence for the moment, what the law says in five European countries, and what happens to footage that has already left the phone.

This page is for the specific moment at a European demonstration when an officer tells you to stop recording, to delete what you have, or to hand over the phone. For the United States, see Can police take your phone or delete your video?. Rules differ by country and by circumstance. Nothing here is legal advice.

 Short answer. If an officer at a protest in Europe tells you to stop filming, delete a video or hand over your phone: stay calm, do not obstruct, say you are filming in a public place, ask for the legal basis of any seizure, note the officer's number and the time, and take legal advice afterwards. In Italy and Germany, our legal pages say a verbal order to delete, with no judicial order, has no legal basis. Footage that Witness Camera already uploaded is in your own cloud storage, not on the phone.

## Do not make it a physical argument

In every country our guides cover, the real limit is obstruction, not the camera. Standing at a reasonable distance with the phone visible is generally protected. Physically getting in the way, or refusing a lawful order to move, is not, whether or not you are filming. Arguing the law at the roadside rarely helps and can turn a calm moment into an arrest.

## Say it once, calmly

 - "I am filming in a public place."

 - If asked to delete: you can say politely that you do not agree to delete anything. Whether an officer can then seize the phone is a separate question that depends on the country and the circumstances.

 - If the phone is being taken: ask for the legal basis, and ask for the officer's identification number.

 - Then stop talking about the law. Your remedies come afterwards, with a lawyer.

## What the law says, country by country

These are the short versions from our legal pages, which give the sources and what we could not verify.

 - Italy. A verbal order to stop recording or delete images, without a seizure order from the judicial authority, has no legal basis. Remaining calm and declining without physical opposition is the firmest position. Italian legal page.

 - Germany. A verbal request to delete the recording has no legal basis without a court or prosecutor's order. Sound is the separate risk, under section 201 StGB. German legal page.

 - France. Filming officers on duty in public is protected expression. In 2021 the Constitutional Council struck down a specific offence on publishing identifiable images of officers. An order given on the ground, even without a legal basis, should be handled calmly. French legal page.

 - Spain. The Constitutional Court held in 2020 that capturing images of officers on duty needs no prior authorisation. Using them in a way that creates a real, proven danger can be an administrative infringement under article 36.23 of Organic Law 4/2015. Spanish legal page.

 - Greece. The Areios Pagos has held that recording police conduct on duty is not within the officer's private life. Publication is weighed case by case. Greek legal page.

## Passcodes and unlocking

Whether you can be required to unlock a phone differs by country and situation, and we have not verified it for the countries above. Ask a lawyer before you need to. What you can do in advance is use a six-digit passcode instead of Face ID or a fingerprint, as the protest phone checklist recommends.

## What to remember, and write down at once

 - The officer's identification number or name, if visible. In France, officers on duty have worn an individual identification number (the RIO) since 2014.

 - The time, the place, what was said, and who else saw it.

 - Write it down as soon as you can. Memory degrades quickly under stress.

## Where your footage is

Witness uploads a piece every 15 seconds to the storage account you connected, hashes each piece and time-stamps the session. Log in to Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud or your WebDAV host from another device to see what arrived. Your emergency contact receives each recording as it is made. Anything that had not finished uploading was still on the phone. The hashes and the time-stamp can be checked by anyone with OpenSSL, without the app.

## Afterwards

 - Contact a lawyer or a legal-support organisation before you publish or hand over anything.

 - Do not edit the original. Work on a copy if you want to blur faces.

 - Blur minors and bystanders before posting online.

## Questions

### Can police in Europe make me delete a video?

 It depends on the country and the situation. Our Italian and German legal pages say a verbal order to delete, with no order from the judicial authority, has no legal basis. For France, Spain and Greece our pages advise handling an order on the ground calmly and asserting your rights afterwards with a lawyer. None of this is legal advice.

### Can police take my phone at a protest?

 In some circumstances, such as a seizure under the relevant procedure, they can. Ask for the legal basis and do not resist physically. Whether and when you must unlock the phone differs by country and we have not verified it.

### Is my footage lost if my phone is seized?

 Not what had already uploaded. Witness sends a piece every 15 seconds to your own storage, so that footage is safe. The piece being recorded and any queued pieces are on the phone.

### Should I argue that I have a right to film?

 Say once that you are filming in a public place, then stop. Debating the law on the spot rarely helps. Your remedies come afterwards, with a lawyer.

# If your teenager goes to a protest: how to prepare their phone
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/teenager-protest-phone-preparation

If your teenager is going to a protest: how to prepare their phone

A plan rather than a ban or a blessing, and the practical steps that matter if something goes wrong.

School and university protests across Europe this autumn have included many under-18s. This page does not say whether a young person should go. It is for parents and guardians who have already decided to stay involved and want the practical side right: a plan, a prepared phone, and honest information about what the app does and does not do.

 Short answer. If your teenager is going to a protest, agree a plan: a meeting point and check-in times, a fully charged phone and a power bank, a lawyer's number written on their arm, and a rule to stay at the edge and leave when told to. Witness Camera is free, rated 4+ on the App Store and Everyone on Google Play, and can share each recording with a contact the user names, which should be agreed with the teenager first.

## Why this matters now

Time reports that, in France, 87% of those detained during the school protests were minors, citing the Justice Ministry. In Turin on 16 October, three minors were arrested for aggravated resistance to a public official, according to the local police headquarters reported by ANSA. We take no side on the demands or on the violence reported by either side. The point is that young people are among those at risk, and preparation helps.

## Talk first

 - Where exactly are they going, and with whom?

 - Agree a meeting point and a check-in time, and what to do if they are separated from the group.

 - Agree the rule: stay at the edge of the crowd, know two exits, and leave when told to by police.

 - Agree what happens if they are detained: who they call, and that they ask for a lawyer.

## Prepare the phone

 - A passcode of at least six digits instead of Face ID or a fingerprint.

 - Fully charged, with a power bank. A dead phone helps nobody.

 - A lawyer's or legal-support number written on their arm in marker, because a number stored in the phone is unreachable if the phone is taken.

 - Your number and the meeting point written down as well.

 - Optional: location sharing with you using your phone platform's own feature, if they agree.

## If they want to film

Many young people will film. The basics are the same as for adults: stay at a reasonable distance, never get in the way of police, keep the phone visible. Our country guides cover the law in five countries. Ask them to blur the faces of other young people before posting anything online, and to keep the original untouched.

## What Witness does, and a privacy point to agree on

Witness Camera (App Store name: Witness: Camera Beyond Reach) is free and works on iPhone and Android. It records with the screen black, uploads every 15 seconds to a cloud account the user owns, and hashes and time-stamps each recording. It is rated 4+ on the App Store and Everyone on Google Play. There is no Witness server, so the developer cannot see the footage.

Its emergency-contact feature shares each recording with a person the user names. If that is you, agree it with your teenager first. Receiving live footage of a protest is a significant privacy matter for them, and a teenager who feels watched may simply not use the tool.

## What parents cannot do from a distance

No app protects someone physically or decides what a court accepts. If your child is detained, contact a lawyer or a legal-support organisation immediately. The rules on detaining minors differ by country and we have not verified them. This page is not legal advice.

## Questions

### Is Witness suitable for teenagers?

 It is rated 4+ on the App Store and Everyone on Google Play. It records video and sound, uploads to a cloud account the user owns, and needs no account with the developer. It is not designed specifically for children, so the user should understand what it does.

### Can I see my child's recordings?

 Only if they choose to name you as their emergency contact or to share their storage with you. Witness has no server, and the developer cannot see or retrieve footage.

### Should my teenager go to the protest?

 We do not take a position. This page is for parents who have decided to stay involved and want the practical preparation right.

### What if my teenager is detained?

 Contact a lawyer or a legal-support organisation immediately. Rules for detained minors differ by country and we have not verified them.

# How to film a dispersal order at a protest: what to capture
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/filming-dispersal-order-protest-europe

How to film a dispersal order at a protest: what to capture

One of the most disputed moments afterwards, and one of the most often missed.

When police order a crowd to disperse, what happens next is argued over for months: whether an order was really given, whether anyone could hear it, whether there was a way out, how long people had. Most footage misses it, because everyone is filming something else. This page is about capturing that moment safely, and about leaving when you are told to.

 Short answer. When police order a crowd to disperse, capture whether an order was actually given and by whom, whether it was audible where the crowd stood, whether it named a way out and whether that way was open, and how long passed before force was used. Film from the edge, say the time aloud when the order is given and again when the line moves, then leave. In France, staying after dispersal orders can itself be an offence (article 431-4 of the Code pénal). Witness Camera uploads every 15 seconds, so what you filmed survives a seized phone.

## What to capture

 - That an order was given, and by whom. Film the person giving it, if you can do so from a safe distance, and anything that identifies who they are.

 - Whether it was audible. Film from where the crowd is standing, pointed towards the source, so the recording captures what could actually be heard at that spot.

 - Whether it named a way out, and whether that way was open. Pan slowly along the route that was announced.

 - The time. Say the time aloud when the order is given and again when the line moves. The gap between the two is what is later disputed. If you worry that your voice would identify you, stay silent and let the time show on the recording instead.

 - The lead-up. The twenty calm minutes before establish that a march was peaceful and where everyone stood.

## Then leave

Filming does not protect you from the consequences of staying. In France, voluntarily remaining in a gathering after the dispersal orders is an offence (article 431-4 of the Code pénal): one year in prison and a €15,000 fine, raised to three years and €45,000 if the face is deliberately concealed, according to the LDH legal note and secondary summaries of the text. Lawyers note that the offence requires the staying to be voluntary, which can be contested if someone did not hear the orders, but that is a defence to raise afterwards, not a plan. The rules differ by country and we have not verified them for the others. Check them for where you are, and when in doubt, go.

## Stay safe while you film

 - Keep two exits in mind and recheck them when the crowd moves. The real danger is being enclosed.

 - Do not move towards the line to get a better shot. Footage from the edge is more useful and safer.

 - Hold the phone visibly and horizontally, and do not use digital zoom. Both are advice from Index, a French digital-investigation NGO.

 - Do not physically obstruct anything. Obstruction, not the camera, is the real legal risk in the countries our guides cover.

## If you are in Germany

Witness always records sound and has no setting to turn the microphone off. German law treats recording the non-publicly spoken word as an offence (section 201 StGB), and whether an officer's announcement at a public operation counts is disputed. See our German legal page. If you want to work without sound, Witness is currently the wrong tool.

## Why upload while recording

A dispersal order is exactly when phones get taken. Witness sends a piece every 15 seconds to storage you own, hashes each piece and time-stamps the session, so the footage of the order is likely to be safe before anyone reaches you. If the queue falls behind on a congested network, it sends a small low-resolution copy of each new piece first. Nothing is deleted from the phone until your storage confirms receipt.

## Questions

### What should I film when police order a crowd to disperse?

 Whether an order was given and by whom, whether it was audible where the crowd stood, whether it named a way out and whether that way was open, and the time when the order was given and when the line moved. Film from the edge and leave when told to.

### Is staying after a dispersal order illegal?

 In France, voluntarily remaining in a gathering after the dispersal orders is an offence under article 431-4 of the Code pénal, with higher penalties if the face is concealed. The rules differ by country and we have not verified them for others. This is not legal advice.

### Can I keep filming after the order is given?

 Do not assume filming protects you. If you stay, you may be committing an offence whether or not you are filming. Comply with the order to leave, and film as you go if it is safe to do so.

### How does Witness help here?

 It uploads a piece every 15 seconds to your own cloud storage, so the footage of the order is likely to have left the phone before it can be taken. It records with the screen black, hashes every piece and time-stamps the session.

# Filming an arrest at a protest: distance, identification, minors
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/filming-an-arrest-at-a-protest-europe

Filming an arrest at a protest: distance, identification, minors

What is useful to capture, where to stand, and what to do with the footage.

An arrest at a demonstration is the moment people most want to film and the moment where filming most often goes wrong: too close, too late, or posted before anyone has taken advice. This page covers the practical side and the limits. At the school and student protests of autumn 2026, many of those detained were minors, which changes what you should do with the footage.

 Short answer. If you see an arrest at a protest, stay at a distance that does not interfere, keep the phone visible, film wide first so the context and numbers are clear, then capture the time, place and any visible identification number or name. Do not approach, interpose or comment at officers, and do not post the footage: give it to a lawyer. If the person detained is a minor, never publish identifiable images. Witness Camera uploads every 15 seconds, so what you filmed survives a seized phone.

## Where to stand and what to capture

 - Stay back. A distance of several metres, ideally with a clear line of sight from the edge of the crowd. Never physically interpose, and never touch anyone.

 - Film wide first. A wide shot with a visible landmark shows how many people and officers were present and where they stood. Then move to a medium shot.

 - Film how it began. The thirty seconds before an arrest are often what is most disputed.

 - Capture identification. Where an officer's number or name is visible, include it. In France, officers on duty have worn an individual identification number (the RIO) since 2014. Rules differ elsewhere: in Germany many but not all states require identification for riot units, and we have not verified Italy, Spain or Greece.

 - Say the time and place once, briefly, unless you prefer silence because your voice could identify you.

 - Do not direct comments at officers. Insulting an officer while filming remains punishable in France, with or without a camera.

## If the person arrested is a minor

In France, 87% of those detained during the school protests were minors, according to the Justice Ministry cited by Time. In Turin on 16 October, the three people arrested were minors, according to the police headquarters reported by ANSA. Filming to document is one thing and publishing is another. Do not post identifiable images of a minor. Keep the original untouched and give it to a lawyer or a legal-support organisation if the family or the young person asks for it. If you publish anything at all, blur the faces of minors and bystanders on a copy.

## What not to do with the footage

 - Do not edit the original. Work on a copy.

 - Do not post straight away. In France, recording and then spreading images of violence is an offence in itself, with an exception for footage made to serve as evidence. The safe route is a lawyer, not a feed.

 - Do not hand it to anyone without thinking about who else it shows. It can identify protesters as well as officers.

## Afterwards

Write down at once what you saw: time, place, what was said, who else was there. Offer the footage to the person's lawyer. Keep the whole Witness session folder, including the manifest and time-stamp proof, which anyone can verify with OpenSSL without the app.

## If you are in Germany

Witness always records sound and has no setting to turn the microphone off, and German law makes recording the non-publicly spoken word an offence (section 201 StGB). See our German legal page.

## Questions

### Can I film an arrest at a protest?

 In the countries our guides cover, filming police on duty in a public place is generally protected, and the real limit is physically obstructing an intervention. Stay back and do not interpose. This is not legal advice.

### What should I capture when filming an arrest?

 Wide context first, how it began, the time and place, and any visible identification number or name. Do not approach and do not comment at officers.

### Should I post a video of an arrest?

 Not straight away. Give it to a lawyer or a legal-support organisation first. If the person is a minor, never publish identifiable images. In France, spreading images of violence is an offence with an exception for footage made as evidence.

### Does an arrest video prove who the officer was?

 Not by itself. Footage without a visible number or name may not identify an officer, which has been a problem in Italian cases. Capture identification where you can do so safely.

# Student and campus journalists: filming protests safely and lawfully
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/student-journalists-filming-protests-europe

Student and campus journalists: filming protests safely and lawfully

The same limits as anyone, a few differences, and a publishing workflow that protects you and the people on camera.

Student reporters are often the ones with the best access to a school or university protest. They face the same limits as everyone else on the street, plus a few questions of their own: whether a journalism exception applies, how to verify what they filmed, and how not to expose the people in it. This page is a practical guide, with the legal points taken from our country pages.

 Short answer. Student and campus reporters filming protests have the same legal limits as anyone, with exceptions that may or may not cover them. In France the offence of recording and spreading images of violence does not apply to the normal exercise of a profession informing the public or to footage made as evidence. Italy's privacy code has a news-reporting exception that does not require a professional card. Greece applies a case-by-case journalism exemption even to non-professionals. Whether a campus outlet counts is not settled in what we checked, so do not assume it. Keep originals, verify, blur minors and have a second person review before publishing.

## The legal points that differ by country

 - France. Recording and spreading images of violence is an offence in itself (article 222-33-3 of the Code pénal, five years and €75,000 for spreading them), but the text does not apply to the normal exercise of a profession whose purpose is to inform the public, or to a recording made to serve as evidence in court. Whether an unpaid student outlet counts as such a profession is not clear from what we read, so ask a lawyer.

 - Italy. The privacy code has an exception for news reporting: sharing an image to communicate news of general interest, without sensationalism or violating dignity. You do not need to be a professional journalist. Minors need particular caution. Italian legal page (in Italian).

 - Germany. Publishing identifiable images without consent can infringe the right to one's own image (sections 22 and 33 KUG). There is an exception for events of contemporary historical interest, but its scope is disputed. Sound is a separate risk under section 201 StGB. German legal page (in German).

 - Greece. The Court of Justice of the EU (case C-345/17, Buivids) held that citizens recording and publishing for a journalistic purpose can fall within the data-protection exemption, even if they are not professionals, assessed case by case, including whether blurring was available. Greek legal page (in Greek).

 - Spain. Filming officers on duty needs no prior authorisation. Using the images in a way that creates a real and proven danger can be an administrative infringement under article 36.23 of Organic Law 4/2015, with respect for the right to information. Spanish legal page (in Spanish).

## A safe workflow

 - Record with provenance. Witness hashes every piece, writes a manifest and time-stamps the session, so you can show the footage is unaltered and dates from when you say.

 - Never edit the original. Work on a copy for cutting and blurring.

 - Check what metadata travels with the file. Witness can record your location in each recording's chain-of-custody record if you allow it. Decide whether that metadata should go out with a published copy.

 - Blur minors and bystanders on the copy, and think about whether a face is needed at all.

 - Get a second person to review before publishing: an editor, a lecturer, or a lawyer for anything involving violence or minors.

 - Do not stream live. Index advises against broadcasting live, and a private upload to your own storage, which is what Witness does, is not a stream.

## Protecting people and sources

Your footage can identify protesters as well as officers. Keep it in storage you control, do not share raw files in group chats, and do not name or tag people. In Italy, the new decree-law 190/2026, in force from 23 October 2026, allows arrests within 48 hours based on video for some offences committed in demonstrations, which makes the handling of raw footage more sensitive still.

## Verification

Anyone can check Witness footage with OpenSSL, without the app, by comparing each file's hash against the manifest and checking the time-stamp token. See how to verify footage. A hash shows a file is unchanged since recording. It does not show that the footage is a fair picture of events.

## Questions

### Do student journalists have a legal exception for filming protests?

 Sometimes, and it is not settled for campus outlets. France exempts the normal exercise of a profession informing the public and footage made as evidence. Italy's news-reporting exception does not require a professional card. Greece applies a case-by-case journalism exemption. Ask a lawyer before relying on any of them.

### How do I show my protest footage is authentic?

 Record with an app that hashes each piece and time-stamps the session, never edit the original, and keep the manifest and time-stamp proof. Witness does this, and the checks can be run with OpenSSL.

### Should I blur faces before publishing protest footage?

 Yes for minors and bystanders, on a copy, keeping the original. A face is rarely needed to tell the story.

### Is it safe to livestream a protest?

 Index advises against filming live. Witness does not stream: it uploads private pieces to your own storage.

# After the protest: who to give footage of police conduct to
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/what-to-do-with-protest-footage-europe

After the protest: who to give footage of police conduct to

Keep the original, take advice first, and know the official routes before you need them.

Footage of police conduct is only useful if it reaches someone who can act on it, in a form that holds up. This page covers what to do with it afterwards and the official routes we could verify in five countries. Procedures change, so confirm them on the official sites, and take legal advice before you hand anything to anyone, authorities included, because the footage may show other people.

 Short answer. After filming police conduct at a protest, keep the original and the full Witness session folder, write down what you saw while it is fresh, and take legal advice before publishing or handing footage over. Routes differ by country. In France: the IGPN (police) or IGGN (gendarmerie) reporting platform, a criminal complaint, or a referral to the Défenseur des droits. In Greece: the Ombudsman acts as the national mechanism for incidents of arbitrariness by police. In Spain: the Defensor del Pueblo has opened inquiries into police charges at protests. In Germany: some states have independent complaint offices and the Bundestag has a federal police commissioner. In Italy, a video alone may not identify an officer.

## First, for every country

 - Keep the original file and the whole session folder: videos, manifest and time-stamp proof.

 - Write down at once what you saw, with the time and place.

 - Do not post it. Take advice from a lawyer or a legal-support organisation you trust, because footage can show other people, including minors.

 - Ask whether the person filmed, or their lawyer, wants a copy.

## Country by country

 - France. The IGPN (police) and IGGN (gendarmerie) have an online reporting platform, but a report on it is not a criminal complaint. A criminal complaint is filed through the IGPN's reception in Paris or at a police station elsewhere. The Défenseur des droits, the independent authority overseeing the conduct of security forces, can be referred to by online form, post or a local delegate. The LDH advises filing a complaint, which lets investigators requisition recordings and a medical examination. Sources: IGPN, LDH.

 - Greece. The Ombudsman acts as the National Mechanism for the Investigation of Incidents of Arbitrariness, competent for complaints about police and coast guard personnel. It does not replace other complaint routes. Confirm the procedure on the Ombudsman's official site.

 - Spain. The Defensor del Pueblo has opened inquiries into police conduct at protests, including after videos of a police charge on a teachers' demonstration in Valencia in May 2026, and admitted a complaint about riot equipment at Ferraz. It asked for the officers involved to be identified. We could not verify the filing procedure.

 - Germany. The Bundestag has had a federal police commissioner since 2024, and several states have independent police complaint offices. Rules on officer identification for riot units vary by state. Amnesty argues that without identifiability convictions are hard. For a criminal complaint, see a lawyer. We could not verify the current position in every state.

 - Italy. We found no verified practical guide. A recent case in Turin illustrates the problem: a young person hit by a tear-gas canister has video of the incident, but prosecutors have sought to close the case because the officers could not be identified, and the lawyer is opposing. Capture units, helmets, numbers, times and places where you safely can, and see a lawyer.

## A caution about your own footage

Footage can identify protesters as well as officers. In Italy, the decree-law of 22 October 2026, number 190, in force from 23 October, allows arrests within 48 hours on the basis of video for some offences in demonstrations, including for minors. It must be converted into law within 60 days and can change. This is one more reason to keep raw footage in your own storage and to take advice before you give it to anyone.

## Questions

### Who should I give footage of police violence at a protest to?

 Take legal advice first. Then the routes depend on the country: in France the IGPN or IGGN, a criminal complaint or the Défenseur des droits; in Greece the Ombudsman; in Spain the Defensor del Pueblo; in Germany independent complaint offices in some states and the federal police commissioner; in Italy a lawyer and the prosecutor. Confirm each on its official site.

### Is a report to the IGPN the same as a complaint?

 No. According to the IGPN's own information, a report on its online platform is not a criminal complaint. A complaint is filed in person, at the IGPN in Paris or at a police station.

### Should I post the video instead?

 Not before taking advice. In France spreading images of violence is an offence with an exception for footage made as evidence, and footage can show minors and other protesters.

### Why keep the whole Witness folder?

 It contains the videos, the manifest with each file's hash and the time-stamp proof, which anyone can verify with OpenSSL without the app. That is what shows the footage is unaltered.

# How to film at a protest: positioning, kettles, mass arrests and what not to post
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/filming-police-protest

How to film at a protest

A crowd is a different job from a single encounter, and the differences are not obvious.

Filming one traffic stop is a problem of framing. Filming a demonstration is a problem of position, timing and, uncomfortably, of everyone else in the shot. The technique that produces good footage of a single arrest can produce footage that gets thirty people identified.

The step-by-step method for filming police is the foundation and this page assumes it. What follows is only what changes when there is a crowd. For the autumn 2026 student protests in Europe, see Filming the police at student protests across Europe.

## Before you leave the house

 01

### Passcode, and a full charge

 Face ID off, six-digit passcode or longer. Then charge to full and bring a power bank, because filming plus a crowded cell tower plus continuous upload is the worst case for a battery and demonstrations run long.

 02

### Expect the network to fail

 Cell capacity at a large demonstration collapses under simple congestion, and it does so exactly when everyone is trying to upload at once. Anything that depends on a live connection should be assumed to be intermittent. Whatever you use to preserve footage should queue on the device and upload when it can rather than failing.

 03

### Write the legal support number on your arm

 In marker, on skin. A number in a phone is a number you cannot reach from a holding cell without your phone. The National Lawyers Guild runs legal support at many US demonstrations and publishes local numbers in advance.

 04

### Decide your job and tell someone

 Documenting and participating pull against each other. If you are there to film, say so to whoever you came with, so nobody is expecting you to be somewhere else when it matters.

## Position, which is most of it

Get height where you can. A step, a wall, a doorway, a first-floor window, a car park deck. Elevation is worth more at a demonstration than at any other kind of filming, because the thing that is disputed afterwards is almost always numbers and geometry: how many people, how far back the line was, who moved first. A shot from ground level in a crowd answers none of that. A shot from four feet up answers all of it.

Film from the edge, not the middle. The middle of a crowd is where you have no exit, no context and no stable frame. The edge gives you the line, the crowd and the space between them in one shot, which is the composition that actually means something.

Know your exit before you need it, and check it again when the crowd moves. The specific hazard at a demonstration is being enclosed: a containment, a blocked side street, a line that closes behind you. If you can see only one way out, you are in the wrong place. This is not primarily about filming; it is about not being arrested for having been standing somewhere.

Do not put your back to a line. Keep officers and the crowd both in your field of view even when you are only filming one of them.

 The single most useful habit: every few minutes, pan slowly across the whole scene and say the time out loud. It costs fifteen seconds and it produces the one thing lawyers consistently cannot get afterwards, which is a reliable record of what the situation looked like immediately before whatever happened next.

## Film the boring part first

The footage people fail to get is not the confrontation. Everyone films the confrontation. It is the twenty minutes beforehand, which is what establishes that a crowd was peaceful, that a street was already blocked, that barricades were placed where they were, that a line formed at a particular time.

So: film the calm. Film the barricades going up. Film the size of the crowd. Film the street layout. Film officers arriving and where they position. None of it is interesting and all of it is the context that makes the interesting part provable.

## Dispersal orders

If an order to disperse is given, that moment is one of the highest-value things you can capture, and it is routinely missed because it happens while everyone is filming something else.

What matters, and what is later disputed:

 - Whether an order was actually given at all, and by whom.

 - Whether it was audible from where the crowd was standing. Film from within the crowd, pointed at the source, so the recording captures what was actually hearable there.

 - Whether it stated a route out, and whether that route was open.

 - How much time passed between the order and enforcement. Say the time when the order is given and say it again when the line moves.

A recording that shows an order was given but was inaudible at the back, and that the named exit was blocked, is worth more than an hour of confrontation footage.

## Mass arrests and containment

If a containment forms, the useful footage changes completely and so does your priority.

Capture the perimeter: where the line is, whether there is any gap, whether people asking to leave are permitted to. Capture time repeatedly. Capture whether food, water or toilets were provided if it goes on for hours; that is frequently the substance of subsequent claims.

During arrests, the thing to get is the pairing: which officer, which person, at what time. That is the link that connects a report to an individual months later and it is very hard to reconstruct from anything else. Badge and helmet numbers, said aloud when you can read them.

 If you are inside the containment, get the footage out of the phone before anything else. A phone taken during a mass arrest may be gone for days, and the recording is on it. This is the situation the app I built exists for, and I would say the same about any of the alternatives: what matters is that footage leaves the device while you are still filming, not after.

## Chemical irritants, projectiles and your own safety

Filming is not protection. If a line advances, if irritants are deployed, if projectiles are used, the correct response is to move, and it does not stop being correct because you are getting a good shot.

Practical points: a camera at eye level is a camera in the path of things aimed at eye level. Contact lenses are a bad idea where irritants may be used. Keep filming while you move rather than stopping to move; a shaky retreat is still evidence and often more informative than a static shot.

## Then the part almost everyone skips

You now have footage full of people who did not agree to be filmed, at a political event, and some of them have specific and serious reasons not to be identified: immigration status, employment, an abusive ex-partner, a protection order, a country they still travel to.

 Blur faces before anything goes public. Signal's image editor detects and blurs faces and is free; you can send a picture to yourself to use it. Apple Photos will let you mark up a still. There are dedicated tools on both platforms for video. Whatever you use, do it before the first post, not after somebody asks.

Two more things follow from that, and they are the ones people get wrong:

 - Keep an unblurred original, untouched. Lawyers need it. Blur the copy you publish.

 - Blurring is a re-encode, so the published version will not match the hash of the original. That is expected and it is why keeping the original matters. Verification runs against what came off the phone.

 - Think about what else is in frame. Placards with names, faces reflected in windows, distinctive tattoos, a licence plate belonging to a participant rather than to police.

WITNESS publishes serious ethical guidance on filming protest and it is worth reading in advance rather than after you have posted something.

## Making sure it survives the day

The failure mode at a demonstration is not that the footage is bad. It is that the phone is taken, dropped, out of battery, or on a network that never uploaded anything.

 Photo library sync generally will not start uploading a video until you stop recording, and defers on cellular besides. At a demonstration, both conditions are usually true at once.

Witness, which I make, uploads in roughly fifteen-second pieces while the recording is still running, to a cloud account you own, queuing on the device when the network is congested and catching up when it is not. Each piece is hashed before it moves. There is more than one app that uploads during recording and I have compared them including where mine loses.

## Afterwards

 - Write it down the same day. Times, badge numbers, what was said, what happened outside the frame.

 - Get footage to legal support if anyone was arrested, before you post any of it.

 - Do not send originals through a messaging app. Re-compression breaks verification. Share links or the files themselves.

 - Consider a records request for body-worn camera footage and dispatch audio. Retention windows for unflagged recordings can be short.

## Related

 - How to film the police, step by step.

 - Can police take your phone or delete your video?

 - What the courts have actually held, including on buffer-zone laws.

 - Setting up before the day.

# Witness for Professionals: how Witness Pro works
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/witness-for-professionals

Witness for Professionals

How Witness Pro works, for journalists, documentary makers, investigators and legal observers.

The free app already does the part that protects footage: it records with the screen black, uploads every 15 seconds to storage you own, and hashes and time-stamps the result. Witness Pro adds picture quality and professional outputs on top of that. It never sits between you and the protection.

## Who Pro is for

Pro is for people who deliver footage to someone else and need more than a phone's default picture: an editor, a broadcaster, an attorney, an investigating body. Typical uses are documentary and investigative work, planned shoots where you control the connection, and coverage that has to go through a newsroom's grading and verification process.

If you are filming an encounter as it happens and getting the footage off the phone matters most, you probably do not need Pro. The free 1080p setting uploads fastest, and that is the setting that survives a seized phone. The field guide covers that case.

## What Pro adds

The two apps share one idea and differ where the platforms do.

 CapabilityiPhoneAndroid

 Resolution1080p (free) or 4K1080p (free) or 4K

 Frame rate24 (cinema), 25 (PAL), 30 or 60 fps24, 25, 30 or 60 fps

 CodecH.264, HEVC 10-bit, ProRes 422 LT or HQH.264, HEVC 10-bit, or Mastering (very high bit rate HEVC)

 Flat colour for gradingApple Log on iPhone 15 Pro and newer, with HEVC or ProRes10-bit HDR (HLG) on phones whose camera supports it, with HEVC or Mastering

 On-screen date, time and locationYesYes, but not together with 10-bit HDR

 One combined video from both camerasYes, on phones that can record bothYes, on phones that can record both

 Shorter cut with the dead air removedYesNot at present

 Evidence packages (PDF report)YesYes

Android has no ProRes encoder on any device, and its public camera interface has no vendor-neutral Log profile. Mastering and 10-bit HDR are the closest equivalents, not the same thing, so an editor expecting ProRes or Apple Log files from an Android phone should say so up front.

## What stays free

 - Recording with the screen black, and starting it in one press.

 - Live upload every 15 seconds to Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud or WebDAV.

 - SHA-256 hashing of every piece and the chain-of-custody manifest.

 - Independent RFC 3161 time-stamping of each session.

 - Sending every recording to an emergency contact as it arrives.

 - Dual-camera recording at 1080p, 30 fps, H.264.

The hashes and time-stamp are in every recording whether Pro is on or off. Anyone can check them with OpenSSL, without the app.

## The trade-off: weight and upload speed

Higher quality costs file size, and file size decides whether footage can leave the phone while you are still filming. The Pro page in the app shows these costs next to each choice. These figures use the same formula the app uses for H.264, HEVC and ProRes, on both iPhone and Android. They are estimates, and real bit rates vary with the scene. Android's Mastering codec is about 100 Mbps at 1080p 30 and scales with resolution and frame rate, so roughly 400 Mbps at 4K 30.

 SettingUpload speed neededPer minuteUploads live

 H.264, 1080p 308 Mbps60 MBYes

 HEVC 10-bit, 1080p 3013 Mbps96 MBYes

 H.264, 4K 3032 Mbps240 MBYes

 HEVC 10-bit, 4K 3051 Mbps384 MBYes

 HEVC 10-bit, 4K 60102 Mbps768 MBYes

 ProRes 422 LT, 1080p 30102 Mbps765 MBNo, stays on the phone

 ProRes 422 HQ, 1080p 30220 Mbps1.6 GBNo, stays on the phone

 ProRes 422 HQ, 4K 30880 Mbps6.6 GBNo, stays on the phone

For comparison, typical LTE gives 5 to 10 Mbps up, and 5G varies a great deal with where you are standing. Below the rate you need, the queue grows for as long as you keep recording. Nothing is lost when that happens: every piece stays on the phone until your storage confirms it, and a small preview copy of each piece goes ahead of the full file so something of every moment is safe early.

 ProRes and Mastering never upload. They run at roughly twenty times the data rate of HEVC, so they are saved to your photo library or gallery on the phone and are not sent to your cloud storage or your emergency contact. If the phone is taken, those recordings go with it. Use them for planned work, not for an encounter you might lose the phone in. The app asks you to confirm before switching to ProRes.

## Both cameras, or the best picture

Recording both cameras at once is limited to 1080p, 30 fps and H.264, and cannot use Apple Log or HDR. If you choose anything above that, only the rear camera records. The app shows which setting turned the front camera off and offers one button to restore the dual-camera settings. When you do record both, Pro can also produce a single video with the front camera as a small inset, in addition to the two separate files.

## Provenance: visible and invisible

Pro can burn the date, time and coordinates into the picture, visible to anyone who watches the video. Some outlets want that on-screen. It is separate from the invisible metadata every recording already carries, which is the SHA-256 hash, the manifest and the independent time-stamp. Turning the burned-in version off removes none of that.

## Evidence packages

An evidence package turns a finished recording into something an attorney or an editor can read. It contains:

 - A PDF report with the recording's start and end times, time zone, number of segments, capture device, first location fix, hashes of each segment and of any merged video, and the steps to verify them.

 - The manifest.json the report describes.

 - The time-stamp proof, where one was obtained.

It contains no video, so it can be shared without exposing the footage. It is built from the phone's own archive, so it works with no network and after the footage has been cleared off the device. Your recordings and their proofs are kept whether or not you have Pro. Pro adds the report.

 What this establishes, and what it does not. The hashes and time-stamp show that a file is unchanged since the phone recorded it and that the manifest existed at a given time. They do not show that the footage is a fair picture of events, and they say nothing about whether a particular court or outlet will accept it. That is a decision for them and for your lawyer.

## Three set-ups worth starting from

These are suggestions, not rules. Check each against your own phone and connection before you rely on it.

 - An event as it happens. Free defaults, or HEVC at 1080p. It uploads while you film. This is the one that protects you if the phone is taken.

 - A planned interview or a documented site. 4K at 24 or 25 fps in HEVC, with Apple Log or 10-bit HDR if you will grade it, on a fast connection or Wi-Fi. Switch on the burned-in timestamp if the outlet wants it.

 - An archive-grade master. ProRes 422 HQ on iPhone or Mastering on Android, filmed from a stable position. It stays on the phone, so copy it off promptly.

## Price and how to get it

On the US App Store, Witness Pro is $1.99 a month, or $29.99 once for a purchase that does not renew and is tied to your Apple ID. Prices vary by country and are always shown in the app. On Google Play, the price is shown in the app and on the listing. Subscriptions are managed or cancelled in your store account settings, and Restore Purchases brings Pro back on a new phone.

## Guides by profession

How Witness fits specific kinds of work, with its limits stated for each.

 - Witness for journalists: footage that survives a seized phone and shows where it came from

 - For newsrooms: how to verify footage recorded with Witness in ten minutes

 - Witness for documentary and investigative filmmakers: picture quality with provenance

Every feature, explained one by one, is on Witness features explained.

## Questions

### Do I need Pro to protect my footage?

 No. Black-screen recording, live upload every 15 seconds, SHA-256 hashing, the chain-of-custody manifest, RFC 3161 time-stamping and emergency contacts are all free and stay free. Pro adds picture quality and a few output formats, nothing that protects footage.

### Can I see what Pro does before I pay?

 Yes. The Witness Pro page in the app shows every control. The controls are inert until Pro is unlocked, so you can read what each one does and what it costs in file size before buying.

### Does 4K upload live during a recording?

 It can, but only if your connection is fast enough. 4K records faster than most mobile networks can send, so the upload queue grows while you film and the last pieces arrive after you stop. Nothing is lost, because every piece stays on the phone until your storage confirms it, and a small preview copy of each piece is sent ahead of the full file. If getting footage out during the event is what matters, 1080p is the setting that does it.

### What happens to ProRes or Mastering recordings?

 They stay on the phone. They are far too large to upload live, so they are saved to your photo library or gallery instead and are never sent to your cloud storage or to an emergency contact. That trades away the protection the rest of the app is built on, so choose it when picture quality matters more than that.

### What happens if I cancel Pro?

 Capture settings that need Pro return to the free defaults, so 4K goes back to 1080p. Your recordings and their proofs are kept either way. A one-time purchase has nothing to renew or cancel.

### What does an evidence package contain?

 A PDF report with the recording's timeline, device details, first location fix, segment hashes and verification steps, plus the manifest.json it describes and the time-stamp proof where one was obtained. It contains no video. The footage stays wherever you already keep it.

The free app is enough to see how everything works. Pro is unlocked from inside it.

# Witness for journalists: footage that survives a seized phone
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/witness-for-journalists

Witness for journalists: footage that survives a seized phone and shows where it came from

Two problems at the moment of recording, and what Witness does about each.

Journalists who cover protests, raids and confrontations face two problems that start before anything is published: losing footage when a phone is taken, damaged or locked, and later being asked to prove the footage is what they say it is. Witness is a free iPhone and Android app that addresses both while you record. This guide is written by the developer of Witness Camera, so read it with that in mind. Everything about other tools comes from their own sites and store listings, and where Witness is the weaker choice, it says so.

 Short answer. Witness Camera records with the screen black, sends a piece every 15 seconds to a Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud or WebDAV account you own, hashes every piece with SHA-256 and has the session independently time-stamped (RFC 3161). For a journalist that means footage can leave the phone before it can be taken, an editor can be given access automatically, and anyone can check the files are unaltered. It does not prove what the footage shows, it always records sound, and it is not a complete security tool. Optional Pro adds 4K, frame rates, Apple Log or HDR and on-screen time and location.

## The two problems

 - Losing the footage. A phone that is taken, smashed or locked takes everything on it. Witness sends each 15-second piece to your own storage as it is recorded, so what had already gone is safe. The piece being recorded and any queued pieces are still on the phone.

 - Proving the footage. A file alone proves little. Witness hashes every piece on the device before it uploads, writes a manifest of hashes, UTC times and location, and has the manifest independently time-stamped when the session ends. A desk can then check it with OpenSSL without trusting the reporter.

## Setting it up as a reporter

 - Connect storage. Google Drive or Dropbox is simplest. A newsroom Nextcloud or WebDAV server keeps footage away from US cloud providers, but WebDAV cannot share automatically, so you share the folder yourself.

 - Name your editor as the emergency contact. With Google Drive or Dropbox they are given access to each recording's folder as footage arrives.

 - Bind a fast start. iPhone: Action Button, Lock Screen widget or Siri. Android: Quick Settings tile, widget or assistant shortcut.

 - Decide on the screen. The default is a black screen. If you want to frame shots, turn the viewfinder on from the Home screen, and you can toggle it while recording.

 - Decide on location. Location ties footage to a place in the record. You can decline it and everything else still works. Some guides advise against it for safety, so decide before the day.

 - Test for 30 seconds and check the file reached your storage.

## What your editor receives

A session folder with the video files, a manifest listing every file's SHA-256 hash, capture times and GPS accuracy, and an independent time-stamp token. Our newsroom guide shows how to check it in about ten minutes.

 What Pro adds for journalists

 - 4K and 24, 25 or 60 fps, for material that will be broadcast or graded.

 - Apple Log (iPhone 15 Pro and newer) or 10-bit HDR on Android, for grading latitude.

 - Visible date, time and location burned into the picture, for outlets that want on-screen provenance. The hash, manifest and time-stamp are in every recording whether this is on or not.

 - A combined video from both cameras, so the reporter and the scene are in one file.

 - Evidence packages: a PDF report with the timeline, hashes and verification steps for a finished recording, plus the manifest and time-stamp proof.

 - Trade-off: higher quality uploads slower. 4K needs a fast connection, and ProRes or Mastering never upload. See how Pro works.

## Where Witness is not enough

 - It does not hide that you are recording. iOS shows its green recording indicator and Android shows a notification. Neither can be hidden.

 - It always records sound, with no setting to turn the microphone off. That matters under some laws, such as German section 201 StGB.

 - Your storage provider is a third party. Footage in Google Drive or Dropbox is reachable by legal process served on them. A newsroom Nextcloud avoids that.

 - It does not use C2PA content credentials. It uses SHA-256 manifests and an RFC 3161 time-stamp. If your outlet requires C2PA, tell your editor.

 - A hash shows a file is unchanged. It does not show that the footage is a fair picture of events. Verification, geolocation and corroboration still belong to your desk.

 - It is not an encryption or concealment tool. For people at serious risk, compare Tella and ProofMode on our comparison page.

## Questions

### Do I need Witness Pro as a journalist?

 No. The free app has black-screen recording, upload every 15 seconds, SHA-256 hashing, the manifest, independent time-stamping and emergency-contact sharing. Pro adds picture quality and outputs such as 4K, Apple Log, on-screen time and location, and evidence packages.

### Can my editor receive my footage automatically?

 Yes with Google Drive or Dropbox: the emergency contact is given access to each recording's folder as it arrives. With WebDAV or Nextcloud there is no automatic sharing, so you share the folder yourself.

### Does Witness support C2PA content credentials?

 No. It uses SHA-256 hashes, a manifest and an independent RFC 3161 time-stamp, which anyone can verify with OpenSSL. C2PA is a different system.

### Is Witness safe for protecting a source?

 Treat it as one layer, not a complete answer. It has no server, but it records sound, shows a recording indicator and stores footage with your chosen cloud provider. Decide about location in advance, and use tools built for concealment if your source is at serious risk.

# For newsrooms: verify footage recorded with Witness in ten minutes
URL: https://witnesscamera.com/verifying-witness-footage-for-newsrooms

For newsrooms: how to verify footage recorded with Witness in ten minutes

What to ask for, three checks, and what each result means.

A contributor says they recorded something with Witness. This page is for the desk that has to decide what that is worth. The checks use standard OpenSSL and a hashing command, not the app, and do not depend on trusting the contributor or the developer. This guide is written by the developer of Witness Camera, so read it with that in mind. Everything about other tools comes from their own sites and store listings, and where Witness is the weaker choice, it says so.

 Short answer. Ask the contributor for the whole Witness session folder (the video files, manifest_.json and timestamp_.tsr), shared by link rather than forwarded through a messaging app that re-encodes video. Hash each video with SHA-256 and compare it with the manifest, run openssl ts -verify on the manifest with the time-stamp authority's CA certificate, then read the token. A pass shows the files are unchanged since the manifest was time-stamped. It does not show what the footage depicts, so geolocation, corroboration and sourcing still apply.

## What to ask the contributor for

 - The whole session folder, not a clip: the video files, manifest_<session-id>.json and timestamp_<session-id>.tsr.

 - Shared by a link to the storage account (Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud) or a direct download, not forwarded through WhatsApp or similar. Re-encoding changes the file, so its hash will no longer match, and that is a mismatch caused by the channel, not by tampering.

 - Ideally with the contributor's name, the time and place they say it was recorded, so you have a claim to test the record against.

## Check 1: do the files match the manifest?

shasum -a 256 recording_rear.mp4 # macOS and Linux
certutil -hashfile recording_rear.mp4 SHA256 # Windows

Open the manifest. Every chunk has a sha256 field, and consolidated videos appear under mergedVideos. The values must match exactly. The manifest also lists capture start and end times in UTC and the GPS coordinates with their accuracy for each chunk.

## Check 2: is the manifest authentic and dated?

openssl ts -verify \
 -data manifest_<session-id>.json \
 -in timestamp_<session-id>.tsr \
 -CAfile <authority-ca-cert>.pem

A pass prints Verification: OK. The manifest names the time-stamp authority in its timestampAuthority field, and the CA certificate comes from that authority's website. A failure here is most often a missing or wrong CA certificate, a local configuration problem, so read the token before concluding anything.

## Check 3: what did the authority actually attest?

openssl ts -reply -in timestamp_<session-id>.tsr -text
shasum -a 256 manifest_<session-id>.json

Confirm that the digest in the token equals the SHA-256 of the manifest file. If it does, a third party with no stake in the matter signed this exact manifest, unmodified, at the time shown. Because the manifest lists every file's hash, that proof extends to the footage.

## What a pass does and does not establish

 - It establishes that the footage existed in this form at that time and has not changed since.

 - It does not establish what the footage shows, or that it was recorded when it appears to have been: only that it cannot postdate the time-stamp.

 - Capture times come from the device clock and are corroborated, not replaced, by the token. Locations come from the phone's GPS and inherit its accuracy.

 - A missing manifest or token means the material is unverified by these means, not that it is false. If the authority was unreachable when the session ended, there is no token.

 - Witness does not use C2PA content credentials. Its provenance is the manifest and the RFC 3161 token.

## What the desk still has to do

Everything a verification desk normally does: geolocate and chronolocate from the picture, corroborate with other sources, check the contributor, and consider context. The record narrows one question, whether the file is what was recorded. For wider practice, see the WITNESS organisation's guidance on video as evidence and the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations, both of which stress authenticity and chain of custody. WITNESS is an unrelated human-rights organisation, not this app.

## Questions

### How do I verify footage recorded with Witness?

 Get the whole session folder, hash each video with SHA-256 and compare with the manifest, run openssl ts -verify on the manifest with the time-stamp authority's CA certificate, and read the token to confirm its digest matches the manifest.

### Why does the hash not match the video I was sent?

 Most often because the video was re-encoded, which messaging apps and social platforms do automatically. Ask for the original files through a link to the storage account.

### Does a verified Witness recording prove the footage is genuine?

 No. It proves the footage existed in this form at that time and has not been altered since. It does not prove what it depicts, so normal verification still applies.

### What if there is no time-stamp file?

 The authority was probably unreachable when the session ended. That is a gap in corroboration, not a sign of tampering. The hashes can still be checked against the manifest.

The free app already has the parts that protect and verify footage. Pro is unlocked from inside it, and its controls are visible before you pay.
